title: Avalokiteshvara
hookLine: the bodhisattva of compassion: Guanyin in China, Kannon in Japan, Chenrezig in Tibet

lines: A VOW TO FREE EVERY BEING.
cards: A bodhisattva has made a vow: not to rest until every being is free of suffering. So he works, and frees beings past counting.
Then he stops, looks out over the world, and sees just as many still suffering as when he began. In that moment of grief, as a Tibetan story tells it, his head splits apart.
It's a startling place for a story about compassion to go. But it doesn't end there.

teach.b: You met this bodhisattva in year one, looking deep in the Heart Sutra, and last year as Guanyin. Today, the whole figure: Avalokiteshvara. First, the remaking.
In the Tibetan telling, the Buddha Amitabha, his teacher, gathers the pieces and makes them into many heads, so he can see suffering in every direction.
Then his arms break too, from reaching for everyone, and Amitabha gives him many arms, with an eye in the palm of each hand.
That's the figure in temples and on thangka paintings: heads rising like a crown, arms fanning out like a halo. Every part answers one question: how do you help when the need is this big?
You see more widely, and you reach in more ways. Second, the names.
In China the Sanskrit name became Guanyin, usually given in English as the one who perceives the sounds of the world. In Japan, Kannon. In Tibet, Chenrezig.
The one known for many eyes is, by name, also the one who hears. Third, the forms.
The Lotus Sutra says this bodhisattva takes whatever form will help: a monk, a king, a child, a woman. And the figure did change from land to land.
In China, Guanyin came more and more to be shown as a woman robed in white. In Japan, Kannon stands at roadsides, in temples and on home altars. Fourth, the honesty of the story.
It admits that caring about suffering can break a person. Its answer isn't to care less.
It's to be put back together with more eyes and more hands, and to keep going.

how: Buddhists across East Asia and Tibet call on Avalokiteshvara by name in times of trouble; Tibetan Buddhists recite the mantra om mani padme hum, and temples in China and Japan keep images of Guanyin or Kannon, some with many arms.

o: the bodhisattva of compassion, who hears the world's cries
a Tibetan king who built the first great monastery
the Buddha of the land of bliss, far to the west

games.q: the one who hears: tap the pairs.
p: to see the need, and to reach it

s: in the Tibetan story, the bodhisattva gives up when his head breaks
Amitabha remakes him with many heads and arms, and he keeps going.
Guanyin, Kannon and Chenrezig are the same bodhisattva
Avalokiteshvara, under the names used in China, Japan and Tibet.
the many arms are only decoration
in the story they are for reaching everyone in need, with an eye in each palm.

games.q: you've vowed to free every being from suffering, and worked without rest. you look out and see as many suffering as when you began. what happens next, in the Tibetan story?
o: your head breaks from grief, and you're remade with more eyes and hands
you hand the vow to someone else
games.why: the story lets the grief be real. then Amitabha remakes him to see in every direction and reach in more ways, and the vow goes on.

practice: Let your eyes close or rest low, and listen to the sounds around you, near ones and far ones.
Then bring to mind the people in your life, one at a time, and listen for what's underneath what they've been saying lately: a tiredness, a worry, a quiet ask they haven't quite made.
You don't need to fix anything; if it starts to feel heavy, come back to the sounds in the room.

wordCard.voice: Avalokiteshvara. The bodhisattva of compassion, Guanyin in China, Kannon in Japan, Chenrezig in Tibet: the one who sees, and hears, and reaches. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the bodhisattva of compassion, carried into Chinese as Guanyin.

carryVoice: Your line: the one who hears. Not less care, but more eyes and more hands. Tomorrow, Manjushri.
